Listen to this article Share Africa’s Mobile Economy Is Growing. Getting People Online Is the Hard Part Mobile technologies and services contributed $240 billion to Africa’s economy in 2025, equivalent to 7.8% of regional GDP, according to the GSMA’s Mobile Economy Africa 2026 report. The report identifies the obstacle facing digital businesses: about 63% of Africa’s population lives within mobile broadband coverage but does not use mobile internet. A further 9% remain outside coverage. The gap between coverage and usage makes a better business starting point than extrapolating from app-download totals alone. For the digital economy in Africa, this distinction affects customer acquisition, pricing, product design and investment. A business serving mobile consumers cannot count every covered phone number as an active market. The immediate commercial question is why users with access to a network are not consistently using online services. The $240 billion figure needs a proper label GSMA estimates that the mobile ecosystem supported approximately 13 million jobs and generated $45 billion in public revenues in 2025. It forecasts mobile’s economic contribution rising to $290 billion by 2030. These totals reflect the wider economic impact of mobile technologies and services, not the revenue of entertainment apps or digital content platforms alone. That distinction matters when reporting business opportunities in Africa’s online services market. A subscription product, streaming service or digital marketplace operates within the larger mobile economy; it does not automatically capture a proportional share of its GDP contribution. Forecasts built by dividing an industry headline across apps would misrepresent the evidence. Coverage is not the same as an affordable transaction GSMA identifies device affordability, digital skills and relevant content among the barriers to mobile internet adoption. A user might have a network signal and still be unable to afford a suitable smartphone, enough data or a recurring subscription. Another may have the hardware but distrust an unfamiliar payment flow. Those obstacles influence conversion before a platform’s marketing campaign even begins. Digital services in Nigeria and neighbouring markets face a practical product challenge: deliver information on ordinary handsets, limit unnecessary data usage and make payment terms understandable. Fast-loading pages and clear account recovery processes do not replace affordable connectivity, yet they can reduce the cost of each successful transaction for customers already online. The business model is moving beyond one-time downloads The online entertainment industry competes for repeat attention. Streaming providers need playable video over variable networks; music services need discoverable catalogues; live sport products need accurate scores delivered without excessive refresh costs. Creators require payment links that work for their audience, not simply a storefront with attractive graphics. The operational metrics worth comparing include: Activation: the proportion of new users completing a meaningful first action. Retention: how many return after seven or thirty days, defined consistently. Data intensity: the megabytes required for a typical session. Payment completion: successful transactions relative to initiated payments. These measures expose whether apparent growth comes from useful activity or repeated promotional downloads. They also make cross-market comparisons more credible than a single count of registrations. Online entertainment is one segment, not the entire story Entertainment choices are widening across video, games, live sport and interactive services, although their economics differ. A sportsbook involves changing event prices, settlement rules and identity checks rather than a subscription catalogue. For instance, Melbet presents a sports-betting service where fixtures and market availability shape the user journey. This is only one product category within the much broader market for mobile experiences. Its verification and regulatory requirements differ from those of streaming. A registered account is not the same as a regularly active customer. Consumer research also matters because mobile platforms are often evaluated through third-party reviews rather than only their home pages. A visitor examining a Melbet review should separate verifiable claims about account functions or betting markets from subjective ratings and promotional statements. A review’s publication date can be important when apps, terms or availability change. Sports-betting interfaces may display decimal odds and in-play markets, but neither an interface feature nor a bonus promises a particular match outcome. Product comparisons need the same source discipline as market-size reports. What a Nigerian product team should test before buying traffic For a service targeting Nigerian customers, the first meaningful test is whether its product works on the devices and connections the intended audience actually uses. Businesses can test low-bandwidth pages, device compatibility and customer-support resolution rates before increasing acquisition spending. Regional language choices and transparent pricing may influence whether a customer returns more than a celebrity campaign. The 2026 GSMA report notes that operators are deploying AI in network optimisation and customer service. Such investments may improve service delivery, but they do not establish that AI-driven apps will instantly eliminate the usage gap. Device financing, network investment and digital literacy still shape the addressable audience. The larger lesson about how mobile technology is transforming the African digital economy is therefore measurable. Mobile’s economic value is rising, yet adoption remains uneven. The next valuable customer may already have network coverage; the company that reduces the cost, effort and uncertainty of the first useful session is better placed to serve them.
